newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed in U.S., Tietmeyer talks up mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed in U.S., Tietmeyer talks up mark.

text.p: Dollar/mark ended lower, extending its slide from Tokyo's new 41-month high after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he believed the dollar's recovery from historic lows in 1995 had concluded.
But a firmer mark/yen cross helped bolster the dollar against the Japanese currency.

The German central bank chief, speaking after the Bundesbank left interest rates unchanged at its biweekly council meeting, also said it was important for the mark to remain strong until it is exchanged for the new single European currency, the euro.
"There was definitely a very strong correlation with Tietmeyer and coming down off the 1.7665 mark high overnight," said Bob Near, a vice president of corporate foreign exchange at Bank of New York.
The dollar fell nearly two pfennigs from the high set in Tokyo, where dealers extended this week's string of powerful gains to another peak not seen since February 1994.
Mark futures buying on Chicago's IMM helped give the dollar an extra shove down to its session low at 1.7463 before finding support, dealers said.

"It was just speculative D-mark interest buying and I think professionals looked at an opportunity to buy some cheap dollars down there," said Ben Strauss, an assistant vice president at Bank Julius Baer and Co.
The dollar ended at 1.7513/18 marks, down from 1.7536/41 at the open and at 113.12/17 yen, up from 112.88/98.
The dollar hit a record low at 1.3438 marks in March 1995 and has risen around 31 percent since then.
This year alone, the dollar has appreciated almost 15 percent against the German currency, driven in large part by fears that the mark would be supplanted by a weak euro.
Following official interest rate hikes by the British and Dutch central banks, the dollar came under further pressure, dealers said.

The dollar's weakness was partly a byproduct of mark buying against the pound, which fell as dealers registered dismay that the Bank of England raised its base rate by only 25 basis points to 6.75 percent, rather than to 7.00 percent as many had anticipated.
The Netherlands raised a key money market rate to 3.0 percent from 2.9 percent.
"In the sterling this was expected but was expected to be higher, so obviously there was disappointment," said Seth Garrett, chief dealer at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp.
"The Dutch news was expected as well, they did sell dollar/mark on that initially but it's not a real reason to sell," Garret continued, referring to the relatively modest size of the hike.
Mark/yen extended its gains a bit from the open, after touching a new two-year low at 63.80 in overnight dealings.

"Mark's downside is now seen solid near 64.50 yen... A Japanese trust bank heavily sold marks against the yen yesterday, so short-covering interest may continue to appear in Tokyo," a trust bank dealer said, adding that dollar/yen may be indirectly supported by a rise in the mark/yen rate.
But a city bank dealer said exporters are keen to sell dollars from 113.20 yen to 113.50 yen in large amounts, capping any dollar gains.
"Traders who had not sold enough dollars previously will be keen to sell dollars for yen on the topside," the trust bank dealers said.
